1. Introduction

Waste systems are integral to modern society. Without them, there would be no unified way to collect, sort, and dispose of the hundreds of millions of tons of waste we produce in the US alone each year (EPA, 2025). Landfills are often the final destination for this waste, but this solution to our trash problem begs another difficult question: where do we put them? 

Landfills, regardless of hazardous status, pose potential health risks to anyone living near them (Weber et al., 2011), but they need to be close to population centers to be efficient in municipal garbage operations. The choice is often made to place landfills near those who have the least influence in government, like lower-income or minority communities (Saha, 2015).

This research will focus on this effect in current day California, the state with the largest sample size, finding out how much the percent of the population that is white, the median household income, the population density, and median home price in a census tract affect the likelihood of it containing a landfill both for all tracts and specifically for urban tracts.

2. Background

Environmental Justice is defined by the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights as the fair treatment of people of all races, income, and cultures with respect to the development, implementation and enforcement of environmental laws, regulations, and policies and their meaningful involvement in the decision-making processes of the government (U.S. Commission on Civil Rights). Meaningful is the key word, as decisions have been openly opposed by communities only to be ignored in the ultimate decision. 

For example In 2015, the disadvantaged and largely latino unincorporated community of Kettleman City was saddled with a further size increase for the hazardous waste landfill located nearby, only one of two in the entire state. The facility admitted waste with high levels of PCBs, (Cabrera, 2024)  chemicals that were used for a variety of industrial purposes until they were banned in 1979. They are known to cause cancer, damage reproductive health and the immune and endocrine systems (EPA, 2025).

According to the environmental organization El Pueblo, the permitting process for the expansion failed to provide court documents to residents in Spanish, and didn’t allow Spanish speakers the same amount of time to talk during court proceedings (Cabrera, 2024). The expansion was ultimately metered by an agreement with the state government, but the initial issue of the dump being located nearby remained the same (Cabrera, 2024).

Another example is the majority black unincorporated community of Snow Hill, North Carolina next to which a landfill was constructed in 1973 (Duke Law, 2025). The community did not have the political authority to stop the construction, and today it is the largest regional dump site in North Carolina. The dumpsite has contaminated the local water supply, and one residence recently tested 8,000 times the EPA’s recommended limit for toxic pollutants known as PFAS (Duke Law, 2025).

There are thousands of different manufactured PFAS chemicals, but the common thread is that they break down very slowly and can build up in organisms. Studies have shown that exposure to certain levels of PFAS can have a myriad of mal effects on human health, including decreased fertility, developmental effects on children, increased risk of cancer, and a reduced immune system (EPA, 2025).

These PFAS chemicals and PCBs are only two categories of pollutants that can come from landfills, and these are just two of numerous (U.S. Commission on Civil Rights) of recorded examples where they and other pollutants impacted a local community.

For this project I am using three separate data sets. The first is the LMOP Landfill and Project Database from the EPA to provide the location of all landfills. It includes the, name, closure status, longitude and latitude, and data about various features of each landfill across the US.

The second is a database of urban developed areas from the US Census Bureau, which includes names, GEOIDs, and geometries for both Urbanized areas (the areas I will consider for this research) and “Urban Clusters,” which are small urban hot spots. I used the package Tigris to access this information.

The final data source is the ACS from the american census bureau which I am using for and data on white population, median household income, and median home price for census tracts in California. I pulled these variables specifically for each census tract in wide format, in addition to the geometries for each census tract.

3.2 Formatting and Spatializing Data

#Filters out only CA data and dumps without location data
trashCA <- trash |>
  filter(State == "CA" & !is.na(Latitude))


#Creates a column that shows percentage of population thats white and also a column for population density
ca_tracts <- ca_tracts |>
  mutate(per_white = (white_popE/total_popE)*100,area_km2 = units::set_units(st_area(geometry), km^2),
    pop_density = total_popE / area_km2)

#Filters urban areas for only urban areas located in California
urban_areasCA <- urban_areasCA|>
  filter(grepl("\\bCA\\b", NAME10) & urban_areasCA$UATYP10 == "U" & GEOID10 != 98020 & GEOID10 != 74179)

For this research it was imperative that all landfills be located in California, and that exact coordinates were available for the landfill. So a tidy filter was applied to the landfill data that kept only rows that contained the California postal code in the NAME column, and where the latitude column was not NA. A similar thing was done with the Urban data for the NAME10 Column, in addition to filtering for only the Urban Areas rows, instead of urban clusters.

Additionally, I added percent white, area in km^2, and then population density columns in the tracts data set to do analysis on them later with a logistic model.

#LANDFILL FORMATTING

#Converts landfill coordinates to Geom point data
trashCA <- trashCA |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(4269)
st_crs(ca_tracts) #Census data already in 4269

##         AXIS["longitude",east,
##             ORDER[2],
##             ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
##     ID["EPSG",4269]]
st_crs(urban_areasCA) #Urban areas already in 
## Coordinate Reference System:
##   User input: NAD83

## GEOGCRS["NAD83",

##             ORDER[2],
##             ANGLEUNIT["degree",0.0174532925199433]],
##     ID["EPSG",4269]]
#URBAN FORMATTING


#Finds if urban areas intersects with each ca_tract and assigns a true or false value
ca_tracts$urban <- lengths(st_intersects(ca_tracts, urban_areasCA)) > 0


#LANDFILL AND TRACT FORMATTING

#Spatial joins CA tracts and trash CA and keeps un matched rows of both as NA for landfills
trashCAT <- st_join(ca_tracts,trashCA, left=TRUE)

#Creates new column that says if there is a landfill in each census tract
trashCAT <- trashCAT |>
  mutate(landfill = ifelse(!is.na(State), TRUE,FALSE))

#Creates a subset of joined data set that only includes data from urban areas
trashCATU <- trashCAT |>
  filter(urban == TRUE)

#Creates subsets of both all tracts and urban subsets that only include rows with landfills
trashCATUT <- trashCATU |>
  filter(landfill==TRUE)
trashCATT <- trashCAT |>
  filter(landfill==TRUE)

In this block I spatialized the trash data by converting the longitude and latitude column to geom point and made sure it is on the same CRS as the other two data sets. Then I added an urban column to the tracts data set that is true if a tract intersects with urban area geometry.

Then I spatially joined the trash data set with the tracts data set, making sure to keep all rows of the tracts data set for proper analyzing with the logistical models. I also created a binary landfill variable that is true if a landfill is present in a tract so that this data set can be used in the logistical models.

Then I created more data subsets of lines that just have landfills so I can use their geom_point data for maps, and also get an idea of the sample size I’m working with.

3.3 Data Exploration and Visualization

3.31 Modeling

#Creates a GLM using all variables as predictors but only using Urban tracts in california
glm_landfillcau <- glm(landfill ~ per_white + med_incomeE + med_home_valE + pop_density, data = trashCATU, family = binomial)
## Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
#Creates a GLM using all variables as predictors using all tracts in california
glm_landfillca <- glm(landfill ~ per_white + med_home_valE + med_incomeE + pop_density, data = trashCAT, family = binomial)
## Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred

For my modeling, I created two logistical models using two different data sets. The first, glm_landfillcau uses only tracts that are within the urbanized areas designated by the census bureau. The second model, glm_landfillca, uses all census tracts within the state of California. Both explore the impact of the four variables on the likelihood of a true outcome for a landfill being in a census tract.

For data visualization I chose to use histograms to best represent the continuous independent variables being measured here, with the number of landfill’s for each bin represented on the Y-axis. This should give a good idea of the distribution of landfills among different values for each variable.

3.32 Mapping

#Creates a map of all CA landfills with Urban area boundaries that intersect with the state of california. Some are mostly not located in the state of california.
  tm_shape(ca_tracts) +
  tm_polygons(col=NULL)+
  tm_shape(urban_areasCA)+
  tm_polygons(fill = "blue")+
  tm_shape(trashCA)+
  tm_dots(fill = "red")+tm_title("Locations of Landfills in California")+
  tm_credits(paste("Author: \nAiden Hall\n","Data Source: \nCensus 2020, EPA 2025"), position = c("right","top"))+
   tm_layout(
    title.size = 1,
    legend.height = 1,
   legend.width = 1,
  )+
  tm_add_legend(type = "symbol",
              labels = "Landfill",
              fill = "red",
              shape = 16,
              size = 0.35,
              position = c("right", "top"))
## [v3->v4] `tm_add_legend()`: use `type = "symbols"` instead of `type =
## "symbol"`.

Because tracts are so small that doing visual mapping analysis of individual tracts at a state level is impractical, further mapping analysis will focus on a couple urban areas. This map shows the location of all landfills in California, so that clusters can be identified and then shown closer up in greater detail. The map shows that there are substantial clusters in the San Jose and Los Angeles urban areas (I identified them independently due to issues with names covering each other up on the map if used).

#Creates a subset of tracts and trash points for San Jose
SJ_Area <- urban_areasCA |> 
  filter(GEOID10 == 79039)
SJ_tracts  <- ca_tracts |>
  st_filter(SJ_Area)
SJ_trash <- trashCA |>
  st_filter(SJ_Area)

#Creates a subset of tracts and trash points for LA
la_Area <- urban_areasCA |> 
  filter(GEOID10 == 51445)
la_tracts  <- ca_tracts |>
  st_filter(la_Area)
la_trash <- trashCA |>
  st_filter(la_Area)

I chose to focus on LA and San Jose in my more focused mapping analysis to demonstrate the general trend of landfill locations in cities. This was due to the identified clusters in the map above. This block of code uses the urban geometries for these two areas to spatially filter tracts and landfill locations to create one map. One limitation of this method is that some rural tracts that barely intersect with the urban areas are represented.

#WHITE PERCENT MAPS

#Finds the median value of percentage of white people in tracts, which is 19.63, rounded up to 20

4. Results

4.1 Model Results

summary(glm_landfillca)

## med_incomeE   -6.636e-06  3.176e-06  -2.089  0.03671 *

#impact on landfill chance for 1 percent increase in white

## [1] -0.0187912

## [1] -0.00661403

## [1] 0.2734884

For the first model, the all tracts model, all of the predictors except median home value are significant based on their sub 0.05 P-values, with population density being extremely significant. Percent white is the least significant with a P-value of 0.01517, though still falling well below the threshold. This means the effect of these variables is unlikely to have occurred by random chance, especially population density. All variables have a negative coefficient, meaning that an increase in them results in a decrease in the chance that there is a landfill in a tract. Population density has an extremely strong effect, with an increase of just 100 people per square kilometer decreasing the chance of a landfill by 19.74%. Far behind that, a $1000 dollar increase in median household income causes a decrease of just 0.73%, and a single percent increase in the white population share of a tract causes a decrease of 0.68%. McFadden’s R squared is 0.3163178, which means this model explains about 31.63% of the variation in the data, making it a strong explanation.

For the second model, the only urban tracts model, all of the predictors except median home value are again significant. However, this time Percent white is extremely significant alongside population density, with a P-value of 0.0000148. This change suggests that within cities there is a significantly higher chance that the percentage of white people in a tract has a real effect. The impact of a percent increase in the share of white people in a tract has also nearly tripled to a decrease in the chance of a landfill of 1.88%. The P-value for median income also increased to 0.03671, though is still significant. This suggests that in cities there is a higher chance that the effect of median income on landfill location is random. The impact also decreased slightly with a 0.66% percent decrease in the chance of a landfill in a tract for an increase of $1000 in the median household income. Population density’s impact also decreased, but still dwarfs the other variables, with a 17.20% decrease in the chance of a landfill for an increase of 100 people per square kilometer. McFadden’s R squared value was 0.2734884, meaning the model explains about 27.34% of the variation in the data. This is weaker than the model using all tracts, but is still a strong explanation.

5. Conclusion

Through this analysis I found that population density is the biggest determiner for the location of a landfill in California, both in urban tracts and all tracts. This was expected, as putting landfills far away from population centers is one solution to the location issue. This research suggests that this is done deliberately with extreme regularity.

However, something that surprised me is that the share of the population that was white also had a significant effect and significance in all tracts and especially urban tracts. What surprised me even more is that median income didn’t have a much bigger significance or impact in all tracts, and actually had a smaller significance and roughly equivalent impact in urban tracts. This suggests that landfills are deliberately placed in tracts with a higher minority population, almost as reliably as it suggests they are placed deliberately in lower income tracts. It also suggests that landfills are placed in tracts with a higher minority population more in cities, where space is limited.

Another thing that surprised me is that median home price wasn’t significant in all tracts or urban tracts. This is likely because it is co-linear with median household income, and so inflated their standard errors which resulted in higher P-values.
